---
title: "Self-supervised Denoising: Noise2Noise, Noise2Self and Noise2Score"
---

## Overview

The previous lectures built generative models that learn a data distribution
directly: GANs through an adversarial game, VAEs through the ELBO, and
normalizing flows through an exact change of variables. This lecture takes a
step sideways to a problem that looks much more modest, image denoising, and
asks a question that turns out to lead straight into the diffusion half of the
course: *can a network learn to remove noise when it has never seen a clean
image?*

We first place denoising inside the general inverse problem and recall the
classical answer (regularized least squares and BM3D) and the first deep
answer (supervised training, DnCNN). Supervised training needs clean targets,
which are often physically impossible to obtain. Three families of methods
avoid them: Noise2Noise trains on pairs of independent noisy copies;
Noise2Self and Noise2Void train on a single noisy copy with a blind-spot
network; SURE trains on a single noisy copy with a divergence penalty. These
look like unrelated heuristics. The second half of the lecture shows that they
are not: Tweedie's formula says that the Bayes-optimal denoiser is determined
by the *score* $\nabla_y \log p(y)$ of the noisy data. For Gaussian noise all
three methods can then be understood through the relation between the score and
the conditional mean that each of them targets. Noise2Score makes this explicit,
estimates the score once, and then applies the Tweedie formula that matches the
noise model (Gaussian, Poisson, Gamma, and others).

The same decomposition --- learn a score during training, use it through
Tweedie's formula at inference --- is the core of diffusion models, which is why
this lecture sits between the VAE/flow lectures and DDPM. After reading this
chapter you should be able to prove why Noise2Noise and Noise2Self do not
collapse, derive SURE from Stein's lemma, derive Tweedie's formula for any
exponential-family noise model, and explain why "denoising is score
estimation".

## Notation

We follow the notation of the slides and of *Geometry of Deep Learning*
[@gdl].

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ | the unknown clean image, flattened to $n$ pixels |
| $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ | the noisy measurement |
| $w$ | additive noise; in the Gaussian case $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ |
| $\mathcal{A}$ | forward (imaging) operator of a general inverse problem |
| $F_\Theta$ | denoising network with parameters $\Theta$; $\hat{x} = F_{\Theta^*}(y)$ |
| $\mathcal{R}(y; \Theta)$, $R_\Theta$ | network in residual form: the DnCNN noise predictor, or a score network |
| $P_Y$ | distribution of the noisy data; $p(y)$ its density |
| $l(y) = \log p(y)$ | log-density of the noisy data |
| $l'(y) = \nabla_y \log p(y)$ | the **score function** of the noisy data |
| $\eta, T(y), p_0(y), \varphi(\eta)$ | natural parameter, sufficient statistic, base measure and log-partition function of an exponential family |
| $l_0(y) = \log p_0(y)$ | log of the base measure; $l_0'(y)$ its derivative |
| $\lambda(y) = \log \frac{p(y)}{p_0(y)}$ | log-ratio appearing in the posterior of $\eta$ |
| $\operatorname{div}_y F$ | divergence $\sum_i \partial F_i / \partial y_i$, the trace of the Jacobian |
| $\sigma_a$ | the *artificial* noise level added in a denoising autoencoder |

References of the form "slide 12" point to the 38-page lecture deck
*Self-supervised Image Denoising* [@lecture-slides-ssl], so that each section can be checked against
the lecture. Norms are Euclidean. The slides write the score both as $l'(y)$ and
$\ell'(y)$; we use $l'(y)$ throughout. A prime on a function of a vector $y$
means its gradient. Expectations without a subscript are over everything that
is random in the expression.

## Denoising as an inverse problem

### The forward model and ill-posedness

An imaging system (slide 3) --- a microscope, a telescope, a CT scanner --- maps an
unknown object $x$ to a measurement through a forward operator $\mathcal{A}$,
and the measurement is corrupted by noise (@fig-inverse):

$$
y = \mathcal{A}(x) + w .
$$ {#eq-forward}

![An imaging system as a forward model. The clean object $x$ passes through the imaging operator $\mathcal{A}$ (here a fluorescence microscope) and noise is added, giving the measurement $y$. Recovering $x$ from $y$ is the inverse problem. From slide 3 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], courtesy of the 2023 ISBI tutorial of Song, Chung and Ye.](figures/lec05/8dgkim-slide-inverse-problem.png){#fig-inverse width=85%}

In the fluorescence microscopy example of the lecture, $\mathcal{A}$ is
convolution with the optical point-spread function, which blurs everything
below the diffraction limit. Recovering $x$ from $y$ is an *inverse problem*,
and it is typically *ill-posed*: many different $x$ produce the same blurred and
noisy $y$, so the data alone do not determine the answer. The question is not
"what is the solution" but "which of the infinitely many candidates is the best
one, and in what sense".

Denoising is the special case $\mathcal{A} = I$:

$$
y = x + w .
$$ {#eq-denoise-model}

It is ill-posed for the same reason --- every $x$ is consistent with $y$ for some
noise realization --- and it is the building block for the general case,
because most modern solvers for @eq-forward alternate a data-consistency
step with a denoising step.

### Classical regularization

The classical remedy (slide 4) restricts the solution space with prior knowledge:

$$
\min_x \; \frac{1}{2}\|y - \mathcal{A}(x)\|_2^2 + \lambda R(x) .
$$ {#eq-regularized}

The first term is the *data fidelity*; the second is a *regularizer* that is
small for plausible images. Common choices in the lecture were sparsity
($R(x) = \|x\|_1$, natural in fluorescence imaging where most pixels are dark),
total variation ($R(x) = \sum_i \|(\nabla x)_i\|$, which favours piecewise-constant
images), and *regularization by denoising* (RED), where an off-the-shelf
denoiser $D$ defines $R(x) = \frac{1}{2} x^\top (x - D(x))$ [@romano2017].

It is worth seeing that @eq-regularized is a Bayesian estimate in disguise,
because the second half of this lecture is entirely Bayesian. With Gaussian
noise $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ the likelihood is
$p(y \mid x) \propto \exp(-\|y - \mathcal{A}(x)\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)$. If the prior is
$p(x) \propto \exp(-\lambda R(x)/\sigma^2)$, Bayes' rule gives

$$
-\log p(x \mid y)
= \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - \mathcal{A}(x)\|^2 + \frac{\lambda}{\sigma^2} R(x) + \text{const},
$$

so minimizing @eq-regularized is the same as maximizing the posterior (MAP
estimation). The regularizer is, up to the factor $\lambda/\sigma^2$ and an
additive constant, a *negative* log-prior. Choosing $R$ by hand is choosing
the prior by hand; learning-based methods instead learn it from data. The
score-based view at the end of this chapter is related but not identical: it
learns the score $\nabla_y \log p(y)$ of the *noisy* data, which differs from the
gradient of the clean log-prior $\log p(x)$ unless the noise vanishes.

### BM3D: collaborative filtering of similar patches

For roughly a decade after its publication, BM3D [@dabov2007] (slides 5--7) was the method to
beat in Gaussian denoising. Its idea is non-local: natural images repeat
themselves, so a small patch usually has many look-alikes elsewhere in the
image (@fig-bm3d-grouping). BM3D works in two stages, each with three steps
(@fig-bm3d-flowchart).

![Grouping by block matching on images corrupted by Gaussian noise ($\sigma = 15$). In each fragment, a reference block is marked "R" and the blocks matched to it are outlined; similar blocks are found along edges and in repeated textures, often far from the reference. From slide 5 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], originally Fig. 1 of @dabov2007.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-bm3d-grouping.png){#fig-bm3d-grouping width=70%}

1. **Grouping by block matching.** For a reference block $R$, search a window
   around it for blocks whose distance to $R$ is below a threshold and stack
   them into a 3D array.
2. **Collaborative filtering.** Apply a 3D decorrelating transform to the stack
   (a 2D transform within each block and a 1D transform across the stack),
   shrink the coefficients, and invert the transform. In stage 1 the
   shrinkage is hard thresholding; in stage 2 it is Wiener filtering, using the
   stage-1 output as a pilot estimate of the signal spectrum.
3. **Aggregation.** Every pixel belongs to many groups, so it receives many
   estimates; these are averaged with weights that favour groups with less
   residual noise.

![The two stages of BM3D. Step 1 groups blocks, applies a 3D transform with hard thresholding and aggregates the block-wise estimates into a basic estimate. Step 2 repeats the grouping on the basic estimate and replaces hard thresholding by Wiener filtering, giving the final estimate. The dashed boxes are repeated for every reference block. From slide 6 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], originally Fig. 3 of @dabov2007.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-bm3d-flowchart.png){#fig-bm3d-flowchart width=100%}

The lecture gave the intuition through principal components: in a stack of
similar blocks, the content shared across blocks lives in a few leading
components, while white noise spreads evenly over all of them, so keeping the
leading components and discarding the rest removes mostly noise. (The original
paper uses fixed transforms such as the DCT and a Haar transform across the
stack rather than PCA, but the reasoning is the same.) On standard test images
at $\sigma = 25$ (input PSNR $20.18$ dB), BM3D reaches $32.08$ dB on *Lena* and
$30.73$ dB on *Barbara*.

The lecture also pointed out a modern reading of BM3D. To process a block, it
finds other blocks that are similar to it and processes them together. That is
what an attention layer does: a query is compared against keys, and the most
similar values are combined. BM3D hand-codes with signal processing what a
transformer learns.

## Supervised denoising and why it is not enough

### The supervised objective

Given pairs $(x, y)$ of clean and noisy images, the most direct approach (slide 8) trains a
feed-forward network to map $y$ to $x$:

$$
\min_\Theta \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\, \ell_{sup}(\Theta),
\qquad
\ell_{sup}(\Theta) = d(x, F_\Theta(y)) = \|x - F_\Theta(y)\|^2 ,
$$ {#eq-sup}

and the trained network is used as $\hat{x} = F_{\Theta^*}(y)$. It is the
simplest and fastest method --- one forward pass per image --- and, as we will
use repeatedly, its population minimizer is known in closed form.

::: {#lem-mmse}
## The squared loss is minimized by the conditional mean

Let $(x, y)$ be jointly distributed with $\mathbb{E}\|x\|^2 < \infty$. Among all
measurable functions $F$, the risk $\mathbb{E}\|x - F(y)\|^2$ is minimized by
$F^*(y) = \mathbb{E}[x \mid y]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $m(y) = \mathbb{E}[x \mid y]$ and expand around it:

$$
\mathbb{E}\|x - F(y)\|^2
= \mathbb{E}\|x - m(y)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|m(y) - F(y)\|^2
  + 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(x - m(y))^\top (m(y) - F(y))\big].
$$

Condition the cross term on $y$. Given $y$, the factor $m(y) - F(y)$ is fixed, and
$\mathbb{E}[x - m(y) \mid y] = 0$ by definition of $m$, so the cross term is zero.
The first term does not depend on $F$ and the second is non-negative and
vanishes exactly when $F = m$ (almost surely).
:::

So a perfectly trained supervised denoiser computes the **posterior mean**, or
minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate. Keep this in mind: every
self-supervised method below will be judged by whether its minimizer is still
$\mathbb{E}[x \mid y]$.

### DnCNN and residual learning

DnCNN [@zhang2017] (slides 9--10) made this work with a deep CNN. Its key design choice is
*residual learning*: instead of predicting the clean image, the network
$\mathcal{R}(y; \Theta)$ predicts the noise $y - x$, and the loss over $N$
training pairs is

$$
\ell(\Theta) = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^N \big\| \mathcal{R}(y_i; \Theta) - (y_i - x_i) \big\|_F^2 ,
$$ {#eq-dncnn}

with the denoised image $\hat{x} = y - \mathcal{R}(y; \Theta)$. The architecture
is a plain stack: Conv+ReLU, then many Conv+BatchNorm+ReLU blocks, then a final
Conv (@fig-dncnn; this is the network we met in the batch-normalization lecture).

![The DnCNN architecture. The input is the noisy image and the output is the *residual*, i.e. the estimated noise, which is subtracted from the input to obtain the denoised image. From slide 9 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], originally Fig. 1 of @zhang2017.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-dncnn.png){#fig-dncnn width=95%}

On the
*castle* image at $\sigma = 50$ (input $14.76$ dB) the slides report BM3D
$26.21$ dB, WNNM $26.51$ dB, EPLL $26.36$ dB and DnCNN $26.90$--$26.92$ dB. The
gains were real but modest, and on texture-rich images early supervised
networks did not consistently beat BM3D, which led to some pessimism at the
time about learned denoisers.

The lecture asked the class what @eq-dncnn reminds us of. A network that takes
a noisy image and outputs the noise component is exactly the
$\epsilon$-prediction network of a diffusion model [@ho2020]. The difference is
in what the network is used for: DnCNN is trained for one noise level
(DnCNN-S) or a range of levels (the blind model DnCNN-B, $\sigma \in [0, 55]$)
and is applied once, whereas a diffusion model is trained across a whole
schedule of noise levels and is applied repeatedly to generate samples. When DnCNN
appeared it was not clear why estimating the noise should be the right thing
to do; Tweedie's formula, below, gives the answer.

### When clean targets do not exist

The weakness of @eq-sup is in its data: it requires matched clean images. In
many scientific problems these do not exist.

- In the black-hole image of the Event Horizon Telescope, nobody has ever seen
  the object, so there is no ground truth at all.
- In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), the electron dose must be kept low to
  avoid destroying the specimen, so every image is very noisy (input SNR around
  $0$ dB) and a clean version cannot be acquired.
- In live-cell or fast-moving imaging, the object moves between exposures, so
  even long exposures or averaging do not produce a clean reference.

Simulated noise is no escape, because real physical noise rarely matches the
simulation. This motivates the question of the lecture: *how can we train a
denoiser without matched clean images?*

## Noise2Noise: learning from pairs of noisy images

### The surprising observation

Noise2Noise [@lehtinen2018] (slides 12--13) replaces the clean target by a *second* noisy
observation of the same image. With two measurements

$$
y_1 = x + w_1, \qquad y_2 = x + w_2 ,
$$

the network is trained to map one to the other (@fig-n2n-n2v, top):

$$
\min_\Theta \; \mathbb{E}\, \|y_2 - F_\Theta(y_1)\|^2 .
$$ {#eq-n2n}

One would expect the network to learn to reproduce noise, since that is what the
targets contain. Instead, at test time it outputs a clean image, and the
quality is almost that of supervised training: in the slides' text-removal
example the network trained on corrupted targets reaches $35.75$ dB against
$35.82$ dB with clean targets.

![Training targets of the self-supervised methods, as drawn in the lecture. Top: Noise2Noise feeds one noisy image to the network and uses a second, independently corrupted image of the same scene as the target. Bottom: Noise2Void uses a single noisy image; the target consists only of a few masked pixels of that same image (the bright squares), and the loss is computed there only. In both cases the output is a clean image although no clean image is ever shown. From slides 12 and 14 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl].](figures/lec05/present091-slide-n2n-n2v.png){#fig-n2n-n2v width=62%}

### Why the minimizer does not change

::: {#thm-n2n}
## Noise2Noise has the supervised minimizer

Assume the second noise is conditionally zero-mean given the input,
$\mathbb{E}[w_2 \mid x, y_1] = 0$, and that all second moments are finite. (This
holds, in particular, when $w_2$ is independent of $(x, w_1)$ and
$\mathbb{E}[w_2] = 0$.) Then for every $F$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\|y_2 - F(y_1)\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|x - F(y_1)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|w_2\|^2 ,
$$ {#eq-n2n-identity}

so the Noise2Noise loss and the supervised loss differ by a constant that does
not depend on $F$, and both are minimized by $F^*(y_1) = \mathbb{E}[x \mid y_1]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Substitute $y_2 = x + w_2$ and expand the square:

$$
\mathbb{E}\|x + w_2 - F(y_1)\|^2
= \mathbb{E}\|x - F(y_1)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|w_2\|^2
  + 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(x - F(y_1))^\top w_2\big].
$$

For the cross term, condition on $(x, y_1)$. The vector $x - F(y_1)$ is then
fixed, so

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(x - F(y_1))^\top w_2\big]
= \mathbb{E}\big[(x - F(y_1))^\top\, \mathbb{E}[w_2 \mid x, y_1]\big] = 0 .
$$

This proves @eq-n2n-identity. The minimizer of the right-hand side is
$\mathbb{E}[x \mid y_1]$ by @lem-mmse.
:::

Two remarks make the statement precise.

- **What is needed is only that the noise in the target averages to zero given
  the input.** The noise need not be Gaussian, need not be independent across
  pixels, and need not have the same distribution as $w_1$. In particular,
  $\mathbb{E}[y_2 \mid y_1] = \mathbb{E}[x \mid y_1]$: the network regresses on the
  noisy target, and the regression function of the noisy target coincides with
  that of the clean one.
- **The price is variance, not bias.** With finitely many training pairs, the
  noisy targets make the empirical loss a noisier estimate of the population
  loss, so more data are needed for the same accuracy.

### Which loss recovers which statistic

The squared loss recovers the mean of the target distribution. Other losses
recover other statistics, and Noise2Noise exploits this to handle noise that is
*not* zero-mean. For a scalar random variable $z$ consider
$c^* = \arg\min_c \mathbb{E}|z - c|^p$.

- **$L_2$ ($p = 2$):** $\frac{d}{dc}\mathbb{E}(z - c)^2 = -2(\mathbb{E}z - c) = 0$
  gives $c^* = \mathbb{E} z$, the mean.
- **$L_1$ ($p = 1$):** for a continuous $z$ with CDF $G$,
  $\mathbb{E}|z - c| = \int_{-\infty}^{c}(c - t)\,dG(t) + \int_c^\infty (t - c)\,dG(t)$,
  so $\frac{d}{dc}\mathbb{E}|z - c| = G(c) - (1 - G(c)) = 2G(c) - 1$. Setting it to
  zero gives $G(c^*) = 1/2$, the median.
- **$L_0$ (mode seeking):** for a discrete target the zero-one loss gives
  $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{z \ne c\}] = 1 - \Pr(z = c)$, so its minimizer is the most
  probable value, the mode. For a continuous target one maximizes instead
  $\Pr(|z - c| \le h)$ for a small window $h$, which approaches a mode of the
  density as $h \to 0$ under regularity conditions. Noise2Noise implements this
  with the surrogate $(|z - c| + \epsilon)^p$ and $p$ annealed from $2$ toward $0$
  during training; this is a practical mode-seeking device, not a theorem that
  the minimizer reaches the mode for every distribution.

![Noise2Noise with non-zero-mean corruptions. Top: random text overlays; the network is trained only on pairs of differently corrupted images (left). The $L_2$ loss leaves a shadow of the mean text colour, while $L_1$ recovers the median and almost matches training with clean targets. Bottom: random-valued impulse noise with $p = 0.70$; only the annealed $L_0$ loss recovers the clean image. PSNR values are under each panel. From slide 13 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], originally from @lehtinen2018.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-n2n-results.png){#fig-n2n-results width=75% fig-pos="H"}

The text-removal and impulse-noise examples on slide 13 (@fig-n2n-results)
show why this matters. A random text
overlay replaces a fraction $p$ of pixels by text colours; the corruption is
not zero-mean, so the $L_2$ loss converges to the average of the clean colour
and the text colours and leaves a visible shadow ($26.89$ dB at $p \approx 0.25$).
When the clean colour is (nearly) determined by the input and $p < 1/2$, it is
still the *median* of the target distribution at each pixel, so the $L_1$ loss
recovers it ($35.75$ dB, against $35.82$ dB with clean targets). For random-valued impulse noise at $p = 0.70$,
even the median is corrupted ($L_2$/$L_1$ give $13.02$/$16.36$ dB); but the clean
value is still the single most likely value, so the annealed $L_0$ loss
recovers the mode and reaches $28.43$ dB, against $28.86$ dB with clean targets.


One caution: the clean-target equivalence of @thm-n2n was proved for the
squared loss only. For $L_1$ there is no general analogue, because adding
independent zero-median noise to an *uncertain* clean value does not preserve
its conditional median. The $L_1$ and $L_0$ results rely on the corruption
leaving the relevant statistic of the target unchanged, which has to be checked
for each corruption model.

### The limitation

Noise2Noise removes the need for clean images, but it still needs *two
independent noisy observations of exactly the same scene*. For a moving object,
a dose-limited specimen or a one-off astronomical event, that is usually as
hard to get as a clean image. The next question is therefore: can we train
from a *single* noisy image?

## Noise2Self, J-invariance and Noise2Void

### Why a single noisy image is a problem

The obvious loss with a single image is the autoencoder loss
$\mathbb{E}\|y - F_\Theta(y)\|^2$. It has a trivial minimizer: the identity
$F(y) = y$ achieves zero loss and removes no noise at all. Any single-image
method must exclude the identity. Two ways are known: restrict the network so
that it *cannot* see the pixel it predicts (this section), or add a penalty
that makes copying expensive (SURE, next section).

### J-invariance

The slides present this idea through Noise2Void; the formal argument below,
from Noise2Self [@batson2019], is added here because it explains why hiding a
pixel rules out the identity. Let
$\mathcal{J} = \{J_1, \dots, J_K\}$ be a partition of the pixel indices
$\{1, \dots, n\}$. For a subset $J$ write $y_J$ for the pixels in $J$ and $J^c$
for its complement.

::: {#def-jinv}
## J-invariant function

A function $F : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is *$\mathcal{J}$-invariant* if for
every $J \in \mathcal{J}$ the output $F(y)_J$ does not depend on the input
$y_J$; that is, $F(y)_J$ is a function of $y_{J^c}$ only.
:::

The identity is not $\mathcal{J}$-invariant, since $F(y)_J = y_J$ depends on
nothing but $y_J$. The point of the definition is the following identity.

::: {#thm-n2s}
## Self-supervised loss for J-invariant functions

Suppose that, given $x$, the noisy pixels in different subsets are independent
($y_J$ is conditionally independent of $y_{J^c}$ given $x$, for each
$J \in \mathcal{J}$), that the noise is zero-mean, $\mathbb{E}[y \mid x] = x$, and
that second moments are finite. Then for every $\mathcal{J}$-invariant $F$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\|F(y) - y\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|F(y) - x\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|y - x\|^2 .
$$ {#eq-n2s}
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand $\|F(y) - y\|^2 = \|(F(y) - x) - (y - x)\|^2$:

$$
\mathbb{E}\|F(y) - y\|^2
= \mathbb{E}\|F(y) - x\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|y - x\|^2
  - 2 \sum_{J \in \mathcal{J}} \mathbb{E}\big[(F(y)_J - x_J)^\top (y_J - x_J)\big].
$$

Fix one $J$ and condition on $x$. By $\mathcal{J}$-invariance, $F(y)_J - x_J$ is a
function of $(y_{J^c}, x)$ only; by assumption $y_{J^c}$ and $y_J$ are
independent given $x$. The conditional expectation of the product therefore
factorizes:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(F(y)_J - x_J)^\top (y_J - x_J) \,\big|\, x\big]
= \mathbb{E}\big[F(y)_J - x_J \,\big|\, x\big]^\top\, \mathbb{E}\big[y_J - x_J \,\big|\, x\big]
= 0 ,
$$

because $\mathbb{E}[y_J \mid x] = x_J$. Taking the outer expectation removes every
cross term.
:::

So, *within the class of $\mathcal{J}$-invariant functions*, minimizing the
self-supervised loss on the noisy image is the same as minimizing the true
error against the unseen clean image. Noise2Noise used independence *between
two images*; Noise2Self uses independence *between pixels of one image*.

Note what the restriction costs. The best $\mathcal{J}$-invariant predictor of
$x_J$ is $\mathbb{E}[x_J \mid y_{J^c}]$, not $\mathbb{E}[x_J \mid y]$: the network
never uses the noisy value of the pixel it is predicting, which still carries
information about that pixel. This is one reason blind-spot methods usually
trail supervised training by a small margin.

### Noise2Void: the blind-spot network in practice

Noise2Void [@krull2019] (slides 14--16) arrived at the same idea from the practical side, in the
setting of microscopy. In a conventional CNN the receptive field of an output
pixel contains the corresponding input pixel; a *blind-spot network* excludes
it (@fig-blind-spot, left). Rather than designing such an architecture,
Noise2Void trains an ordinary CNN with a masking scheme (@fig-blind-spot,
right; target of @fig-n2n-n2v, bottom):

1. pick a random set $M$ of pixels in a training patch;
2. replace each $y_i$, $i \in M$, by the value of a randomly chosen neighbour
   *other than $i$ itself*, giving a modified input $\tilde{y}$;
3. compute the loss only on the masked pixels:
   $\sum_{i \in M} (F_\Theta(\tilde{y})_i - y_i)^2$.

Because the network never sees the original $y_i$ at a masked location, it
cannot copy it, and the argument of @thm-n2s applies to the masked pixels. In
the lecture's exaggerated picture, the network is shown an image with holes and
learns to fill the holes from the context; because the noise in a hole is
independent of its context, the best it can do is predict the clean value. One
caveat: at test time the image is fed *without* masks, so the guarantee of
@thm-n2s describes training; only an architectural blind spot keeps
$\mathcal{J}$-invariance at inference.

![The blind spot in the original Noise2Void paper. Left, (a) and (b): in a conventional network the prediction for a pixel depends on a patch of input pixels that includes the pixel itself (blue cone), so training with the same noisy image as input and target yields the identity; a blind-spot network excludes the pixel from its own receptive field. Right, (a) to (c): the masking scheme used in training. In a patch (b) of the noisy image (a), a randomly selected pixel (blue) is copied into the masked location (red); the target (c) is the unmodified noisy patch, and the loss is computed only at the masked pixels. From slide 15 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], originally Fig. 2 and 3 of @krull2019.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-blind-spot.png){#fig-blind-spot width=100%}

The slides compare Noise2Void with BM3D, supervised training ("traditional")
and Noise2Noise. On BSD68 the PSNRs are $28.59$ (BM3D), $29.06$ (supervised),
$28.86$ (Noise2Noise) and $27.71$ dB (Noise2Void); on simulated cell-membrane
data they are $29.96$, $32.56$, $32.43$ and $32.28$ dB. Noise2Void gives up a
little accuracy, but it needs neither clean nor paired data. On real cryo-TEM
and fluorescence data, where no clean target exists and often no second noisy
copy either, only BM3D and Noise2Void are applicable at all, and Noise2Void is
much faster at inference (about $0.1$--$1.3$ s against $4.6$--$33.2$ s for
BM3D on the slides' examples).

A student asked how the model knows which part of the image is noise. The
answer is that it does not need to: the model assumes every pixel is signal plus
noise, and the independence of the noise is the only thing that distinguishes
the two. *Under that independence assumption*, whatever the network can predict
from the context must come from the signal, because the noise at a pixel
carries no information about its neighbours. When the noise is spatially
correlated this breaks down, and the network also predicts the correlated part
of the noise (see @sec-independence).

The lecture also asked what masking pixels and predicting them reminds us of.
It is masked token prediction, as in masked language modelling (and, at the
level of representations, JEPA). At the end of the lecture this resemblance is
revisited as an analogy: both predict hidden content from its context, which
for continuous images is tied to the score, while for discrete tokens it is an
analogy rather than a theorem.

## SURE: a single image with a divergence penalty

### Stein's unbiased risk estimate

The second way to exclude the identity keeps the plain autoencoder loss and adds
a penalty. For Gaussian noise $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$, the SURE
denoiser [@soltanayev2018] (slides 17--19) minimizes

$$
\ell_{SURE}(\Theta) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\, d(y, F_\Theta(y)),
\qquad
d(y, F_\Theta(y)) := \|y - F_\Theta(y)\|^2 + 2\sigma^2 \operatorname{div}_y F_\Theta(y) .
$$ {#eq-sure}

The first term is the autoencoder loss; the second, the *divergence-based
penalty*, is large for the identity, whose divergence is $n$. The construction
comes from classical statistics, where Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE)
[@stein1981] was used for decades, for example to tune wavelet thresholds,
before deep learning. The key fact is Stein's lemma.

::: {#lem-stein}
## Stein's lemma

Let $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$ and let $g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be
weakly differentiable with $\mathbb{E}|\partial g_i / \partial y_i| < \infty$. Then,
for fixed $x$ and $y = x + w$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[w^\top g(y)\big] = \sigma^2\, \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{div}_y g(y)\big].
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
It suffices to prove the scalar identity
$\mathbb{E}[w_i\, g_i(x + w)] = \sigma^2\, \mathbb{E}[\partial_i g_i(x + w)]$ for each
coordinate and sum over $i$. Fix all coordinates except $w_i$; the density of
$w_i$ is $\phi(t) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2} e^{-t^2 / 2\sigma^2}$, which satisfies
$t\, \phi(t) = -\sigma^2 \phi'(t)$. Integrating by parts,

$$
\int t\, \phi(t)\, g_i(\dots, x_i + t, \dots)\, dt
= -\sigma^2 \Big[\phi(t)\, g_i\Big]_{-\infty}^{\infty}
  + \sigma^2 \int \phi(t)\, \partial_i g_i(\dots, x_i + t, \dots)\, dt .
$$

The boundary term vanishes under mild growth conditions (for example, if $g_i$
grows at most polynomially; @stein1981 gives the precise conditions). Taking the expectation over the other
coordinates gives the claim.
:::

::: {#thm-sure}
## SURE is unbiased for the true error

Under the assumptions of @lem-stein, and if $\mathbb{E}\|F(y)\|^2 < \infty$, for any fixed $x$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\|F(y) - x\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\Big[\|y - F(y)\|^2 + 2\sigma^2 \operatorname{div}_y F(y)\Big] - n\sigma^2 .
$$ {#eq-sure-identity}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $F(y) - x = (F(y) - y) + w$ and expand:

$$
\mathbb{E}\|F(y) - x\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\|F(y) - y\|^2 + 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[w^\top (F(y) - y)\big] + \mathbb{E}\|w\|^2 .
$$

The last term is $n\sigma^2$. For the middle term,
$\mathbb{E}[w^\top y] = \mathbb{E}[w^\top x] + \mathbb{E}\|w\|^2 = n\sigma^2$, and
$\mathbb{E}[w^\top F(y)] = \sigma^2\, \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{div}_y F(y)]$ by Stein's lemma.
Hence the middle term is $2\sigma^2 \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{div}_y F] - 2n\sigma^2$, and
collecting terms gives @eq-sure-identity.
:::

As a sanity check, the identity $F(y) = y$ has zero autoencoder loss but
divergence $n$, so its SURE value is $2n\sigma^2 - n\sigma^2 = n\sigma^2$, exactly the true
error of not denoising: the penalty removes the identity's artificial
advantage. The right-hand side of @eq-sure-identity can be evaluated
*without $x$*. It is unbiased only in expectation; for one image it can even be
negative, and a very flexible network can overfit it on a small dataset. The
constant $-n\sigma^2$ does not affect the minimizer, which is why @eq-sure drops
it. Because the identity holds for every fixed $x$, it also holds after
averaging over $x$, so minimizing @eq-sure over networks is minimizing the
supervised risk.

### Computing the divergence: Monte-Carlo SURE

For a network with millions of outputs, $\operatorname{div}_y F_\Theta$ is the trace
of an $n \times n$ Jacobian and cannot be formed explicitly. The SURE denoiser
uses the Monte-Carlo estimate of @ramani2008: draw $\tilde{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$
independent of $y$ and use, for a small $\epsilon > 0$,

$$
\operatorname{div}_y F(y) \approx \frac{1}{\epsilon}\, \tilde{n}^\top \big(F(y + \epsilon \tilde{n}) - F(y)\big).
$$ {#eq-mc-div}

To see why, Taylor-expand $F(y + \epsilon \tilde{n}) - F(y) = \epsilon\, J_F(y)\, \tilde{n} + O(\epsilon^2)$,
where $J_F$ is the Jacobian. Then the right-hand side of @eq-mc-div equals
$\tilde{n}^\top J_F(y)\, \tilde{n} + O(\epsilon)$, and since $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{n}\tilde{n}^\top] = I$,

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{n}}\big[\tilde{n}^\top J_F(y)\, \tilde{n}\big] = \operatorname{tr}\big(J_F(y)\, \mathbb{E}[\tilde{n}\tilde{n}^\top]\big) = \operatorname{tr} J_F(y) = \operatorname{div}_y F(y) .
$$

One extra forward pass per training step is enough; the randomness of
$\tilde{n}$ averages out over training like the randomness of a minibatch. @fig-sure-check checks both @eq-sure-identity and @eq-mc-div numerically.

On one BSD68 image at $\sigma = 50$ (input $14.76$ dB) the slides report BM3D $26.14$ dB,
a SURE-trained network $26.46$ dB, and the same network trained with clean
targets (MSE) $26.85$ dB: SURE does not reach supervised quality, but it is
close and it needs no clean data.

## A side-by-side comparison

Slide 20 puts the three approaches next to each other.

- **Supervised learning:** $\ell_{sup}(\Theta) = \|x - F_\Theta(y)\|^2$, with
  noisy-clean pairs $(x, y)$.
- **Noise2X** (Noise2Noise, Noise2Self, Noise2Void, ...):
  $\ell_{selfsup}(\Theta) = \|z - F_\Theta(y)\|^2$, where the target $z$ is
  derived from the noisy data in a way specific to each algorithm: a second
  noisy copy, the masked pixels, or (in Noisier2Noise [@moran2020]) the original
  $y$ when the input is an even noisier version of it.
- **SURE:** $\|y - F_\Theta(y)\|^2 + 2\sigma^2 \operatorname{div}_y F_\Theta(y)$, a
  divergence penalty compensating for the use of $y$ itself as target.

Written this way, the losses differ mainly in the target ($x$, $z$ or $y$),
together with what each method adds to make that target usable: an independent
second copy, a restriction on what the network may see, or the divergence
penalty. These algorithmic choices look heuristic and unrelated, and each comes with its own
proof. Is there a *unified mathematical theory* of self-supervised denoising
--- one that explains why all of them work and points to something better? The
answer of @kim2021 is Tweedie's formula.

## Tweedie's formula

### Exponential families and their posteriors

Following slides 22--23, a family of densities $p(y \mid \eta)$ indexed by a parameter $\eta$ is an
**exponential family** if it can be written as

$$
p(y \mid \eta) = p_0(y)\, \exp\!\big(\eta^\top T(y) - \varphi(\eta)\big),
$$ {#eq-expfam}

where $p_0(y)$ depends on $y$ only, $T(y)$ is the *sufficient statistic*, $\eta$ is
the *natural parameter*, and $\varphi(\eta)$ depends on $\eta$ only and makes the
density integrate to one. The parameter enters only through the cross term
$\eta^\top T(y)$. Gaussian, Poisson, Gamma, Bernoulli and exponential
distributions are all of this form, as the table in @sec-tweedie-table shows.
The decomposition is not unique (we will see two for the Gaussian), but the
result below does not depend on the choice.

Put a prior $p(\eta)$ on the parameter. Bayes' rule gives the posterior

$$
p(\eta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \eta)\, p(\eta)}{p(y)}
= \frac{p_0(y)}{p(y)}\, \exp\!\big(\eta^\top T(y)\big)\, e^{-\varphi(\eta)}\, p(\eta),
$$

and absorbing $p_0(y)/p(y)$ into the exponent,

$$
p(\eta \mid y) = \exp\!\big(\eta^\top T(y) - \lambda(y)\big)\, \big[p(\eta)\, e^{-\varphi(\eta)}\big],
\qquad
\lambda(y) = \log \frac{p(y)}{p_0(y)} ,
$$ {#eq-posterior}

where $p(y) = \int p(y \mid \eta) p(\eta)\, d\eta$ is the marginal density of the
data. The posterior is itself an exponential family, now in $\eta$, with the
roles of parameter and statistic exchanged: the cross term is again
$\eta^\top T(y)$, and the bracket depends only on $\eta$.

### The closed form of the posterior mean

Under squared loss the Bayes-optimal estimate of $\eta$ is the posterior mean
$\hat{\eta} = \mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y]$ (@lem-mmse). The remarkable fact, due to
Robbins and Tweedie and popularized by @efron2011, is that this posterior mean
can be written in terms of the marginal density of $y$ alone.

::: {#thm-tweedie}
## Tweedie's formula for exponential families

Let $y$ be scalar, let $p(y \mid \eta)$ have the form @eq-expfam with $T$
differentiable, and assume $p(y)$ and $p_0(y)$ are positive and differentiable
and that differentiation in $y$ may be exchanged with integration in $\eta$.
Then

$$
\hat{\eta}^\top T'(y) = \lambda'(y) = -\nabla_y \log p_0(y) + \nabla_y \log p(y) = -l_0'(y) + l'(y) ,
$$ {#eq-tweedie}

where $\hat{\eta} = \mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y]$ and $T'(y)$ is the derivative of the
sufficient statistic. The quantity $l'(y) = \nabla_y \log p(y)$ is the
**score function** of the noisy data.
:::

::: {.proof}
The posterior @eq-posterior integrates to one for every $y$:

$$
\int \exp\!\big(\eta^\top T(y) - \lambda(y)\big)\, p(\eta)\, e^{-\varphi(\eta)}\, d\eta = 1 .
$$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $y$. The bracket
$p(\eta) e^{-\varphi(\eta)}$ does not depend on $y$, and the derivative of the
exponent is $\eta^\top T'(y) - \lambda'(y)$, so

$$
\int \big(\eta^\top T'(y) - \lambda'(y)\big)\, p(\eta \mid y)\, d\eta = 0 .
$$

The first part of the integral is $\mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y]^\top T'(y)$; the second is
$\lambda'(y)$ because $p(\eta \mid y)$ integrates to one. Hence
$\hat{\eta}^\top T'(y) = \lambda'(y)$. Finally,
$\lambda(y) = \log p(y) - \log p_0(y) = l(y) - l_0(y)$, which gives the
right-hand side of @eq-tweedie.
:::

Read @eq-tweedie from right to left. The noise model fixes $T$ and $p_0$, which
are known. The only thing that depends on the unknown clean-image distribution
is the score $l'(y)$ of the *noisy* data --- and the noisy data are exactly what
we have. If we can estimate the score from noisy images, we obtain the
Bayes-optimal estimate of $\eta$ without ever seeing a clean image.

For an image $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $T(y) \in \mathbb{R}^k$, the same proof
differentiates with respect to each $y_i$. Writing $J_T(y) \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}$
for the Jacobian of $T$, the result is

$$
J_T(y)^\top\, \mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y] = \nabla_y \log p(y) - \nabla_y \log p_0(y).
$$ {#eq-tweedie-vector}

When the noise acts independently on each pixel, $J_T$ is (block) diagonal and
this is the scalar formula applied pixel by pixel; the score $\nabla_y \log p(y)$,
however, still depends on the whole image, because the clean-image prior does
not factorize. Two cautions follow from the form of @eq-tweedie-vector. The
score determines $\mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y]$ only through the linear map $J_T^\top$,
which sends $\mathbb{R}^k$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$; recovering an unrestricted
$k$-dimensional $\mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y]$ needs this map to be injective, i.e.
$\operatorname{rank} J_T = k$ ($J_T$ has full *row* rank). Known components of $\eta$
can supply the missing information, as for $\eta_1 = \alpha - 1$ in the Gamma
case below. And $\mathbb{E}[\eta(x) \mid y]$ is
in general not $\eta(\mathbb{E}[x \mid y])$ when $\eta$ is a nonlinear function of $x$;
we meet both points in the Poisson and Gamma cases below.

### Case 1: Gaussian noise

Let $y = x + w$ with $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ and $\sigma$ known (slides 24--25). Expanding the
square in the Gaussian likelihood separates the $y$-only, cross and $x$-only
terms:

$$
p(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{(y - x)^2}{2\sigma^2}}
= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2}}}_{p_0(y)}
  \exp\!\Big(\underbrace{\frac{x}{\sigma^2}}_{\eta}\, \underbrace{y}_{T(y)} - \underbrace{\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}}_{\varphi(\eta)}\Big).
$$

So $\eta = x/\sigma^2$, $T(y) = y$ with $T'(y) = 1$, and
$l_0(y) = -\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2} + \text{const}$, whence $-l_0'(y) = y/\sigma^2$.
Substituting into @eq-tweedie,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\eta \mid y] = \frac{\hat{x}}{\sigma^2} = \frac{y}{\sigma^2} + l'(y),
$$

and multiplying by $\sigma^2$,

$$
\boxed{\;\hat{x} = \mathbb{E}[x \mid y] = y + \sigma^2\, l'(y), \qquad l'(y) = \nabla_y \log p(y).\;}
$$ {#eq-tweedie-gauss}

For an image with $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ the same computation holds pixel by
pixel, with $l'(y) = \nabla_y \log p(y) \in \mathbb{R}^n$. More generally, for
correlated Gaussian noise $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ the vector decomposition
$\eta = \Sigma^{-1}x$, $T(y) = y$, $l_0(y) = -\frac{1}{2} y^\top \Sigma^{-1} y + \text{const}$ gives
$\Sigma^{-1}\hat{x} = \Sigma^{-1} y + \nabla_y \log p(y)$, that is
$\hat{x} = y + \Sigma\, \nabla_y \log p(y)$; we return to this when we discuss
correlated noise.

The decomposition is not unique. The second Gaussian row of the table uses
$\eta = [x/\sigma^2, -1/(2\sigma^2)]^\top$, $T(y) = [y, y^2]^\top$ and
$p_0(y) = 1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, so that $l_0' = 0$ and $T'(y) = [1, 2y]^\top$. Then @eq-tweedie reads $\hat{x}/\sigma^2 - 2y/(2\sigma^2) = l'(y)$, which is again @eq-tweedie-gauss. The term that was in $p_0$ has moved into $\eta^\top T$, and
the answer is unchanged.

**Denoising is score estimation.** @eq-tweedie-gauss can be read in
both directions:

$$
l'(y) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[x \mid y] - y}{\sigma^2},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[w \mid y] = y - \mathbb{E}[x \mid y] = -\sigma^2\, l'(y).
$$ {#eq-score-denoiser}

An MMSE denoiser and the score of the noisy distribution determine each other.
The second identity answers the question left open by DnCNN: a network trained
to predict the noise from $y$ converges to $\mathbb{E}[w \mid y]$, which is the
score scaled by $-\sigma^2$. Predicting noise, predicting the clean image and
predicting the score are the same task. @fig-tweedie-1d verifies @eq-tweedie-gauss on a two-component Gaussian mixture.

**A direct check without exponential families.** In the Gaussian case the
formula can also be verified by differentiating the marginal
$p(y) = \int \mathcal{N}(y; x, \sigma^2 I)\, p(x)\, dx$ under the integral. Since
$\nabla_y \mathcal{N}(y; x, \sigma^2 I) = -\frac{y - x}{\sigma^2}\, \mathcal{N}(y; x, \sigma^2 I)$,

$$
\nabla_y p(y) = \int \frac{x - y}{\sigma^2}\, \mathcal{N}(y; x, \sigma^2 I)\, p(x)\, dx
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\nabla_y \log p(y) = \frac{\mathbb{E}[x \mid y] - y}{\sigma^2},
$$

after dividing by $p(y)$ and recognising the posterior $p(x \mid y)$ inside the
integral. This is @eq-score-denoiser again, in any dimension.

**A simple closed-form case.** If $x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau^2)$, then
$y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau^2 + \sigma^2)$ and $l'(y) = -(y - \mu)/(\tau^2 + \sigma^2)$, so
Tweedie gives $\hat{x} = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2} y + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2}\mu$, the
familiar Wiener shrinkage. With $\mu = 0$, $\tau^2 = 4$, $\sigma^2 = 1$ and $y = 3$, the
score is $-0.6$ and $\hat{x} = 3 + 1 \cdot (-0.6) = 2.4$; the Bayes risk is
$\tau^2\sigma^2/(\tau^2 + \sigma^2) = 0.8$ against $1$ for the raw observation.

### Case 2: Poisson noise

Photon-limited imaging (low-light fluorescence, astronomy, PET; slide 26) produces counts:
$y \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ with mean $x > 0$,

$$
p(y \mid x) = \frac{x^y e^{-x}}{y!} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{y!}}_{p_0(y)} \exp\!\big(\underbrace{\log x}_{\eta}\cdot \underbrace{y}_{T(y)} - \underbrace{x}_{\varphi(\eta) = e^\eta}\big).
$$

Here $\eta = \log x$, $T(y) = y$ and $T'(y) = 1$. To differentiate in $y$ we
extend $p(y)$ and $p_0(y)$ smoothly to real $y$, using $y! = \Gamma(y + 1)$. Then
$l_0(y) = -\log \Gamma(y + 1)$ and $l_0'(y) = -\psi(y + 1)$, where $\psi$ is the
digamma function. The asymptotic expansion
$\psi(z) = \log z - \frac{1}{2z} + O(z^{-2})$ gives
$\psi(y + 1) = \log(y + \frac{1}{2}) + O(y^{-2})$, which is the approximation on the
slides:

$$
l_0'(y) \approx -\log\!\big(y + \tfrac{1}{2}\big).
$$

Substituting into @eq-tweedie gives the exact relation and its approximation,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\log x \mid y] = \psi(y + 1) + l'(y) \approx \log\!\big(y + \tfrac{1}{2}\big) + l'(y),
$$

and writing $\log \hat{x}$ for the right-hand side,

$$
\boxed{\;\hat{x} = \big(y + \tfrac{1}{2}\big) \exp\!\big(l'(y)\big).\;}
$$ {#eq-tweedie-poisson}

One subtlety deserves to be stated. Tweedie's formula gives the posterior mean
of the *natural parameter*, here $\log x$. So @eq-tweedie-poisson is
(approximately) $\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log x \mid y])$, the posterior *geometric* mean,
which by Jensen's inequality is never larger than $\mathbb{E}[x \mid y]$; the
digamma approximation adds a further error at small counts. The worked example
of @sec-worked-poisson measures both gaps.

For comparison, the exact posterior mean of $x$ also has a closed form in terms
of the marginal, without any derivative (Robbins' formula; see @efron2011). Since
$x \cdot \frac{x^y e^{-x}}{y!} = (y + 1)\frac{x^{y+1} e^{-x}}{(y+1)!}$,

$$
(y + 1)\, p(y + 1) = \int x\, \frac{x^y e^{-x}}{y!}\, p(x)\, dx
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb{E}[x \mid y] = (y + 1)\, \frac{p(y + 1)}{p(y)} .
$$

For counts, a ratio of neighbouring probabilities plays the role that the
score plays for continuous data. Note that the two formulas estimate different
quantities: Robbins' ratio gives the arithmetic posterior mean exactly, whereas @eq-tweedie-poisson approximates the geometric one (compare the columns of @tbl-poisson below).

### Case 3: Gamma noise

Multiplicative noise --- speckle in ultrasound and synthetic aperture radar, for
instance --- is modelled by a Gamma distribution whose scale is proportional to
the clean value. Following slide 27, write

$$
p(y \mid x) \propto \Big(\frac{y}{x}\Big)^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta \frac{y}{x}}
= \exp\!\Big( (\alpha - 1)\log y - \frac{\beta}{x}\, y - (\alpha - 1)\log x \Big),
$$

with $\alpha, \beta$ known. This is the model $y = x\, n$ with multiplicative noise
$n \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)$ (shape $\alpha$, rate $\beta$); the change of variables
$n = y/x$ contributes a factor $1/x$, and the normalized density is

$$
p(y \mid x) = \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)\, x^\alpha}\, y^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta y / x}, \qquad y > 0,
$$

with $\mathbb{E}[y \mid x] = \alpha x / \beta$. The noise has mean one when $\alpha = \beta = k$,
which is the setting "Gamma ($k = 100$)" of the experiments below. The
$x$-only factors are absorbed in $\varphi(\eta)$, which plays no role in @eq-tweedie. The parameter enters
through two cross terms, so $\eta$ and $T$ are vectors:

$$
p_0(y) = 1, \qquad
\eta = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha - 1 \\ -\beta / x \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
T(y) = \begin{bmatrix} \log y \\ y \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
T'(y) = \begin{bmatrix} 1/y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

(The summary table on the slides lists $T(y) = [\log y, -y]^\top$; with
$\eta_2 = -\beta/x$, the sign that reproduces $e^{-\beta y / x}$ is $T_2(y) = y$, as on
the derivation slide.) Since $l_0' = 0$, @eq-tweedie gives

$$
\frac{\alpha - 1}{y} - \beta\, \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{x} \,\Big|\, y\Big] = l'(y).
$$

Writing $\beta/\hat{x}$ for $\beta\,\mathbb{E}[1/x \mid y]$ and solving for $\hat{x}$,

$$
\boxed{\;\hat{x} = \frac{\beta y}{(\alpha - 1) - y\, l'(y)}.\;}
$$ {#eq-tweedie-gamma}

Here $\hat{x}$ is the posterior *harmonic* mean, $1/\mathbb{E}[1/x \mid y]$, again
because the natural parameter is $-\beta/x$ rather than $x$. For an exact score the denominator
$(\alpha - 1) - y\, l'(y) = \beta y\, \mathbb{E}[1/x \mid y]$ is positive; with an
estimated score it can approach zero or change sign, which an implementation
has to guard against.

A conjugate example checks both the algebra and the interpretation. Take the
prior $x \sim \text{InverseGamma}(a_0, b_0)$, with density proportional to
$x^{-a_0 - 1} e^{-b_0 / x}$. Multiplying by the likelihood gives the posterior
$\text{InverseGamma}(a_0 + \alpha,\, b_0 + \beta y)$, and integrating $x$ out gives
$p(y) \propto y^{\alpha - 1} (b_0 + \beta y)^{-(a_0 + \alpha)}$, so
$l'(y) = \frac{\alpha - 1}{y} - \frac{\beta (a_0 + \alpha)}{b_0 + \beta y}$. With
$a_0 = 2$, $b_0 = 1$, $\alpha = \beta = 4$ and $y = 1$: $l'(1) = 3 - 4.8 = -1.8$, and @eq-tweedie-gamma gives $\hat{x} = 4/(3 + 1.8) = 5/6$. The posterior is
$\text{InverseGamma}(6, 5)$, whose harmonic mean is $b/a = 5/6$ (exactly the
formula) and whose mean is $b/(a - 1) = 1$.

### The full table {#sec-tweedie-table}

Repeating the computation for other members of the family gives the table of @kim2021 (slide 28). It is split here into the decompositions
(@tbl-expfam) and the resulting estimators (@tbl-tweedie), with the Gamma sign
corrected and the Gamma density normalized as above.

| Distribution | $p(y \mid x)$ | $\eta$ | $T(y)$ | $p_0(y)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$ | $x/\sigma^2$ | $y$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2}}$ |
| Gaussian (alt.) | same | $[\frac{x}{\sigma^2}, -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}]^\top$ | $[y, y^2]^\top$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ |
| Poisson | $\frac{x^y e^{-x}}{y!}$ | $\log x$ | $y$ | $\frac{1}{y!}$ |
| Gamma$(\alpha, \beta)$ | $\frac{\beta^\alpha y^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha) x^\alpha} e^{-\beta y/x}$ | $[\alpha - 1, -\frac{\beta}{x}]^\top$ | $[\log y, y]^\top$ | $1$ |
| Bernoulli | $x^y (1 - x)^{1 - y}$ | $\log\frac{x}{1 - x}$ | $y$ | $1$ |
| Exponential | $x e^{-yx}$, $y \ge 0$ | $-x$ | $y$ | $1$ |

: Exponential-family decompositions of common noise models. {#tbl-expfam}


| Distribution | $l_0'(y)$ | Tweedie estimate $\hat{x}$ | What $\hat{x}$ is |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | $-y/\sigma^2$ | $y + \sigma^2 l'(y)$ | posterior mean |
| Gaussian (alt.) | $0$ | $y + \sigma^2 l'(y)$ | posterior mean |
| Poisson | $\approx -\log(y + \frac{1}{2})$ | $(y + \frac{1}{2}) \exp(l'(y))$ | approx. posterior geometric mean |
| Gamma$(\alpha, \beta)$ | $0$ | $\frac{\beta y}{(\alpha - 1) - y\, l'(y)}$ | posterior harmonic mean |
| Bernoulli | $0$ | $\frac{e^{l'(y)}}{1 + e^{l'(y)}}$ | logistic of posterior mean of $\eta$ |
| Exponential | $0$ | $-l'(y)$ | posterior mean of the rate |

: Tweedie denoisers obtained from @tbl-expfam by solving $\hat{\eta}^\top T'(y) = -l_0'(y) + l'(y)$. {#tbl-tweedie}

The last two rows are one line each. For the exponential distribution,
$p(y \mid x) = \exp(-x\, y + \log x)$, so $\eta = -x$, $T = y$, $p_0 = 1$, and @eq-tweedie gives $\mathbb{E}[-x \mid y] = l'(y)$, i.e. $\hat{x} = -l'(y)$; here
$\hat{x}$ is the genuine posterior mean of $x$ because $\eta$ is linear in $x$. For
the Bernoulli distribution, $\eta = \log\frac{x}{1-x}$ and $\hat{\eta} = l'(y)$; mapping
back through the inverse of the logit gives the sigmoid in the table (which,
as in the Poisson case, is the image of the posterior mean of $\eta$, not the
posterior mean of $x$; for a binary $y$ the derivative must again be understood
through a smooth extension).

The message of the table, highlighted on the slides, is: **as long as we can
compute the score function, optimal denoising can be achieved by Tweedie's
formula**, for every noise model in the family. "Optimal" here has a precise
meaning: the formula gives the posterior mean of the natural parameter, which
is optimal for squared error *in that parameter*. It is the MMSE estimate of
$x$ itself when $\eta$ is linear in $x$ (Gaussian, exponential), and a geometric,
harmonic or logistic posterior summary otherwise (Poisson, Gamma, Bernoulli).

## Noise2Score

### Training once, denoising by formula

Noise2Score [@kim2021] (slide 29) turns the table into an algorithm with two phases.

1. **Training phase (noise-model agnostic).** Train a network $R_\Theta$ on
   noisy images only so that $R_{\Theta^*}(y) \approx l'(y) = \nabla_y \log p(y)$.
2. **Inference phase (noise-model specific).** Plug the estimated score into
   the Tweedie formula of @tbl-tweedie for the noise model at hand
   (@fig-noise2score).

![The Noise2Score pipeline. A network $R_{\Theta^*}$ trained on noisy images outputs an estimate of the score $l'(y)$; Tweedie's formula for the noise model at hand turns the score into the estimate $\hat{x}$. From slide 29 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl].](figures/lec05/8dgkim-slide-n2score-pipeline.png){#fig-noise2score width=75%}

The noise model and its parameters ($\sigma$, or $\alpha$ and $\beta$) enter only in
the second phase, and the training procedure is the same whatever the noise.
This should not be read as "one trained network serves every noise model".
The network learns the score of the observed distribution $p(y)$, and $p(y)$
depends on the noise: data with Poisson noise and data with Gaussian noise
have different marginals and need their own score networks (or one network
conditioned on the noise). What the separation buys is that, for a given
dataset, the noise model is needed only at inference, and the same training
code applies to every noise type.

This decomposition --- learn the score of a distribution during training,
design the downstream use at inference --- is precisely the structure of
diffusion models. There, too, training only learns a score, and sampling is a
separate algorithm built on top of it; the difference is that diffusion
sampling iterates (denoise with Tweedie, then add a little less noise), while
Noise2Score denoises deterministically in one step. What remains is the
training phase: how do we estimate the score from noisy samples?

## Estimating the score from noisy data

### The score function

For a density $p_{data}(x)$ (slide 31), the score $\nabla_x \log p_{data}(x)$ is a vector field: at
every point it points in the direction in which the density increases fastest,
towards the nearby modes, with a magnitude that is large where the density
changes quickly relative to its value (@fig-score). It is the same object that diffusion models learn.
Two features make it convenient: it does not depend on the normalizing constant
of $p$, since $\nabla \log (c\, p) = \nabla \log p$, and it can be estimated from
samples. Before diffusion models, two classical estimators were known.

![A two-mode density (left) and its score (right). Each arrow points in the local direction of steepest increase of the log-density, and the arrows vanish at the modes. From slide 31 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl]; the slide credits Yang Song's blog post on score-based generative modelling.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-score.png){#fig-score width=70%}

### Denoising autoencoders estimate the score

The first is the denoising autoencoder (DAE). In the form shown on slide 32
[@alain2014], we take the *noisy* data $y$, corrupt it further with artificial
Gaussian noise of level $\sigma_a$, and train the network to recover $y$:

$$
\ell_{DAE}(\Theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\substack{y \sim P_Y \\ u \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \\ \sigma_a \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \delta^2)}} \big\| y - F_\Theta(y + \sigma_a u) \big\|^2 .
$$ {#eq-dae}

Note that this is a Noise2X loss: the input is a modified version of $y$, the
target is $y$.

::: {#prp-dae}
## The optimal DAE is a score estimator

Fix the artificial noise level $\sigma_a$ and let $p_{\sigma_a} = p * \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_a^2 I)$
be the density of $\tilde{y} = y + \sigma_a u$. The minimizer of @eq-dae at this
level is

$$
F_{\Theta^*}(\tilde{y}) = \tilde{y} + \sigma_a^2\, \nabla \log p_{\sigma_a}(\tilde{y}),
$$

and as $\sigma_a \to 0$,

$$
F_{\Theta^*}(y) = y + \sigma_a^2\, l'(y) + o(\sigma_a^2).
$$ {#eq-dae-score}
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-mmse the minimizer is $F^*(\tilde{y}) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid \tilde{y}]$. The pair
$(y, \tilde{y})$ is exactly a "clean signal plus Gaussian noise" pair, with $y$ in
the role of the clean signal and $\sigma_a$ in the role of $\sigma$, so the Gaussian
Tweedie formula @eq-tweedie-gauss applies to it with the marginal density
$p_{\sigma_a}$ of $\tilde{y}$:
$\mathbb{E}[y \mid \tilde{y}] = \tilde{y} + \sigma_a^2 \nabla \log p_{\sigma_a}(\tilde{y})$.
For the limit, $p_{\sigma_a}$ solves the heat equation, so
$p_{\sigma_a} = p + \frac{\sigma_a^2}{2}\Delta p + o(\sigma_a^2)$ for smooth $p$, and therefore
$\nabla \log p_{\sigma_a} = \nabla \log p + O(\sigma_a^2)$. Multiplying by $\sigma_a^2$ gives @eq-dae-score.
:::

The score is then read off from the residual,
$\hat{l}'(y) = (F_{\Theta^*}(y) - y)/\sigma_a^2$. Subtracting two nearly equal images
and dividing by a tiny $\sigma_a^2$ is numerically fragile, so in practice the
network is parameterized in residual form,
$F_\Theta(\tilde{y}) = \tilde{y} + \sigma_a^2 R_\Theta(\tilde{y})$. For a *fixed* level
$\sigma_a$, substituting $\tilde{y} = y + \sigma_a u$ into @eq-dae gives

$$
\ell_{DAE}(\Theta) = \sigma_a^2\, \mathbb{E}\, \big\| u + \sigma_a R_\Theta(y + \sigma_a u) \big\|^2 ,
\qquad
R_{\Theta^*}(\tilde{y}) = -\frac{\mathbb{E}[u \mid \tilde{y}]}{\sigma_a} = \nabla \log p_{\sigma_a}(\tilde{y}),
$$

so $R_\Theta$ is trained directly as a score network. Three cautions keep the
argument honest. First, at a fixed $\sigma_a > 0$ the DAE learns the score of the
*smoothed* density $p_{\sigma_a}$, and only its rescaled residual converges to
$l'$ as $\sigma_a \to 0$; at $\sigma_a = 0$ the task is the plain autoencoder and the
identity is optimal. Second, the slide samples $\sigma_a \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \delta^2)$; a network
that is not told $\sigma_a$ then learns a weighted mixture of smoothed scores, so
the fixed-scale result holds for it only approximately. Third, the auxiliary level $\sigma_a$ is used only to *learn*
the score; denoising the real image uses the physical noise level,
$\hat{x} = y + \sigma^2 R_{\Theta^*}(y)$, and confusing the two gives the wrong
correction. Two further observations follow.

- **The limit is Tweedie for Gaussian noise.** @eq-dae-score has
  exactly the form $y + \sigma^2 l'(y)$ of @eq-tweedie-gauss. The lecture asked
  the class where we had seen this formula before; this is the answer. A DAE
  trained at level $\sigma_a$ outputs the Tweedie denoiser for Gaussian noise of
  level $\sigma_a$.
- **Noise2X methods are related to score estimation.** Noisier2Noise [@moran2020] adds
  further noise to the noisy image and regresses back to it, which is the DAE
  loss with $y$ as target; Moran et al. then apply a correction that depends on
  the noise model (for additive noise of the same level, $2F(z) - z$) to reach
  the clean signal, and their method is not restricted to Gaussian noise. Noise2Noise has the
  same population minimizer as supervised training (@thm-n2n), the MMSE
  denoiser, and for Gaussian noise that denoiser determines the score through @eq-score-denoiser, so a perfectly trained Noise2Noise network *is* the
  Gaussian Tweedie denoiser. Blind-spot methods target the restricted
  conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[x_J \mid y_{J^c}]$ instead, which is related to, but in
  general not equal to, the Tweedie denoiser. This is the sense in which the
  lecture explains these methods through the score.

  As the lecture added, this reading is specific to Gaussian noise.

### SURE is implicit score matching

The second classical estimator is score matching [@hyvarinen2005] (slide 33). Plug the
residual form

$$
F_\Theta(y) = y + \sigma^2 R_\Theta(y), \qquad \hat{l}'(y) = \frac{F_{\Theta^*}(y) - y}{\sigma^2} = R_{\Theta^*}(y)
$$

into the SURE loss @eq-sure. (Slide 33 writes $\sigma_a$ here; in SURE the level
is the physical noise level $\sigma$, so we write $\sigma$.) The autoencoder term becomes
$\|y - F_\Theta(y)\|^2 = \sigma^4 \|R_\Theta(y)\|^2$, and the divergence is
$\operatorname{div}_y F_\Theta = \operatorname{div}_y y + \sigma^2 \operatorname{div}_y R_\Theta = n + \sigma^2 \operatorname{div}_y R_\Theta$.
Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{SURE}(\Theta)
&= \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\big\{ \|y - F_\Theta(y)\|^2 + 2\sigma^2 \operatorname{div}_y F_\Theta(y) \big\} \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\big\{ \sigma^4 \|R_\Theta(y)\|^2 + 2\sigma^4 \operatorname{div}_y R_\Theta(y) \big\} + 2\sigma^2 n \\
&= 2\sigma^4\; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\Big\{ \tfrac{1}{2}\|R_\Theta(y)\|^2 + \operatorname{div}_y R_\Theta(y) \Big\} + 2\sigma^2 n .
\end{aligned}
$$

Up to the positive factor $2\sigma^4$ and an additive constant, this is the
**implicit score matching** loss of Hyvarinen (2005) with $\Psi_\Theta = R_\Theta$:

$$
\ell_{ISM}(\Theta) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\Big\{ \tfrac{1}{2}\|\Psi_\Theta(y)\|^2 + \operatorname{div}_y \Psi_\Theta(y) \Big\}.
$$ {#eq-ism}

::: {#thm-ism}
## Implicit score matching estimates the score

Assume that $p > 0$ is differentiable, that $\Psi_\Theta$ is (weakly) differentiable,
that $\mathbb{E}\|\Psi_\Theta(y)\|^2$, $\mathbb{E}|\operatorname{div}_y \Psi_\Theta(y)|$ and
$\mathbb{E}\|\nabla_y \log p(y)\|^2$ are finite, and that the boundary terms of the
coordinatewise integration by parts vanish (for example,
$p(y)\Psi_\Theta(y) \to 0$ as $\|y\| \to \infty$). Then

$$
\ell_{ISM}(\Theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y} \|\Psi_\Theta(y) - \nabla_y \log p(y)\|^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbb{E}_{y \sim P_Y}\|\nabla_y \log p(y)\|^2 ,
$$

so @eq-ism is minimized by $\Psi_\Theta = \nabla_y \log p = l'$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand the square:
$\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\Psi - \nabla \log p\|^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\Psi\|^2 - \mathbb{E}[\Psi^\top \nabla \log p] + \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla \log p\|^2$.
For the middle term use $p\, \nabla \log p = \nabla p$ and integrate by parts in
each coordinate; the boundary terms vanish by assumption:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\Psi^\top \nabla \log p] = \int \Psi(y)^\top \nabla p(y)\, dy = -\int \operatorname{div}\Psi(y)\, p(y)\, dy = -\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{div}\Psi] .
$$

Substituting and rearranging gives the claim.
:::

So the SURE network, written in residual form, is trained to output the score,
and the denoised image it produces is $y + \sigma^2 l'(y)$, once more the Gaussian
Tweedie formula (by @thm-ism). The lecture's conclusion (slide 34): **Noise2X and SURE are score-based
approaches.** For Gaussian noise, a DAE learns the score of a smoothed density,
SURE in residual form learns the score of $p(y)$ itself, and Noise2Noise
learns the MMSE denoiser that is equivalent to that score; blind-spot methods
learn a restricted version of the same conditional mean.

For Gaussian noise the link is exact in three places: any MMSE denoiser
determines the score through @eq-score-denoiser, a DAE identifies the score of
the smoothed density, and SURE in residual form *is* implicit score matching.
(The Noise2Noise and Noise2Self identities themselves do not need Gaussian
noise; Gaussianity is what makes the conversion to a score simple.) The
lecture extended the analogy to masked token prediction in language models
and to diffusion models: in its reading, much of the success of modern
self-supervised learning comes from the same decomposition into score
estimation at training time and a well-designed downstream task at inference
time. For discrete tokens this is an analogy between prediction tasks rather
than a theorem about continuous image scores.

### Results

Because Noise2Score separates score estimation from the denoising formula, it
can use the correct formula for each noise model. Slides 35--36 compare it with
a noise-specific self-supervised baseline (SURE for Gaussian, its
Poisson analogue PURE, Noise2Void for Gamma) and with Noise2Self. @fig-results shows the first set of images and @tbl-results collects the
PSNR values of both slides.

![Noise2Score ("Ours") against the ground truth (GT), a noise-specific baseline (SURE, PURE or Noise2Void) and Noise2Self (N2S) for Gaussian noise ($\sigma = 50$), Poisson noise ($\zeta = 0.05$) and Gamma noise ($k = 100$). The number in each panel is its PSNR in dB; the insets magnify the boxed region. From slide 35 of the course slides [@lecture-slides-ssl], originally from @kim2021.](figures/lec05/present091-slide-results.png){#fig-results width=75% fig-pos="H"}

| Noise | Image | Noisy | SURE / PURE / N2V | Noise2Self | Noise2Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 50$ | 1 | $15.26$ | $27.13$ (SURE) | $28.14$ | $28.71$ |
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 50$ | 2 | $15.12$ | $26.59$ (SURE) | $27.60$ | $28.18$ |
| Poisson, $\zeta = 0.05$ | 1 | $18.01$ | $25.19$ (PURE) | $25.52$ | $26.04$ |
